div.p:
The Cyrenaeans urged Plato to write laws for them and leave them behind and to set their constitution in order, but he declined, saying that it was difficult to legislate for the Cyrenaeans when they were so prosperous; for nothing is by nature so haughty and harsh and hard to rule as a manNauck. p. 617 when he lays hold of what seems to be good fortune. That is why for rulers it is difficult to become an adviser concerning rule; for they are afraid to accept reason as a ruler, lest it curtail the advantage τἀγαθὸν *: τὸ ἀγαθὸν of their power by enslaving it to duty. For they do not know the saying of Theopompus, the king of the Spartans, who was the first in Sparta to join the Ephors with those who ruled as kings, and then, being reproached by his wife on the ground that he would hand down to his children a lesser rule than the one he had received, said, Greater, rather, inasmuch as it is also more secure. For by giving up what was excessive and absolute in it he escaped the danger together with the envy. And yet Theopompus, by diverting the power of rule to others as if it were a great stream, cut off from himself as much as he gave to others.
But the reason that comes from philosophy and is settled in the ruler as his assessor and guardian removes the hazardous element from his power, as from robust health, and leaves what is sound.

But most kings and rulers, having no sense, imitate the unskilful sculptors, who think that their colossal figures appear φαινεῖσθαι Madvigius great and massive if they model them with legs set very wide apart and straining and gaping. For these men too seem, by heaviness of voice and harshness of look and moroseness of manners and unsociableness of life, to imitate the majesty and dignity of sovereignty, though they differ not at all from colossal statues, which have a heroic and godlike form outside, but inside are full of earth and stone and lead; except that in the case of the statues these weights keep their uprightness permanent and unbending, whereas uneducated generals and rulers are often rocked and capsized by the folly within them; for, building a lofty power on a foundation not laid straight, they lean over together with it. But just as the rule itself*: αὐτὸν , having been made straight and undistorted, thus straightens the other things, assimilating συνεξομοιῶν (46, 100): συνεφομοιῶν unde συναφομοιῶν W them to itself by fitting them to it and laying them alongside it, so in like manner the ruler must first himself αὐτὸν] om. mei gain the τὴν R rule within himself, straighten his soul ψυχὴν idem: ἀρχὴν and establish his character, and so make his subjects fit him.
For it is not for one who is falling to set others upright, nor for one who is ignorant to teach, nor for the disorderly to bring order, or for the undisciplined to impose discipline, or for one who is not ruled to rule. But most people, thinking wrongly, believe that the first good in ruling is not being ruled; and indeed the king of the Persians regarded all as slaves except his own wife, of whom he ought most of all to have been master.

Who, then, will rule the ruler? Law, the king of all, mortals θνατῶν Pindarus (Bergk. 1 p. 439): θηντῶν and immortals, as Pindar said; not law writtenM: γεγραμμένοις outside in books or on some wooden tablets, but reason that is alive within him ἐν αὐτῷ Coraes: ἑαυτῷ aut ἐν ἑαυτῷ , always dwelling with him and watching over him and never leaving his soul bereft of guidance. For the king of the Persians had one of his chamberlains appointed for this purpose, to come in at dawn and say to him, Arise, O king, and attend to the matters which you should attend to, as the great Oromasdes μέγας Ὠρομάδης Kaltwasserus: μεσορομάσδης cf. Vit. Artax. c. 29 willed. But within the educated and self-controlled ruler is the one who always says this and exhorts him. For Polemo said that love is the service of the gods for the care and preservation καὶ σωτεηρίαν addidi ex compar. Thes. et Rom. c. 2 of the young. But one might more truly say that rulers serve God for the care and preservation of men, so that of the fine and good things which God gives to men they may distribute some and guard the others.
Do you see this boundless sky on high, Nauck. p. 663
which holds the earth around in its moist embrace ἔχοντα αὐταῖς ἀγκάλαις mei? The one sends down the beginnings of the appropriate seeds, and the earth sends them up, and they grow, some by showers, some by winds, some warmed by the stars and the moon, but the sun adorns all things and mingles in all things that famous love-charm which comes from himself αὐτοῦ *: αὐτοῦ . But of such τοιούτων *: τοσούτων cf. Stob. 46, 101 and so great gifts and blessings as the gods bestow there is no enjoyment nor right use without law and justice and a ruler. Now justice is the end of law, and law is the work of the ruler, and the ruler is the image of God who orders all things, not needing a Phidias to mould him, nor a Polycleitus or a Myron, but himself making himself into a likeness to God through virtue and creating the most pleasant of statues to behold and the most godlike. And as God has set up in heaven the sun, a most beautiful image of himself, and the moon, such a likeness and light in states is the ruler who, god-fearing, upholds good justicecf. Hom. τ 109. 111, that is, one who, having the reason of God, has intelligence καὶ διάνοιαν R, sed recte se habet vulgata, not a sceptre or a thunderbolt or a trident, as some mould and paint themselves, making their folly invidious by aiming at the unattainable.
For God is indignant at those who imitate thunders and thunderbolts and rays of light, but those who emulate his virtue and make themselves like him in what is good and humane he gladly makes to prosper, and gives them a share of the good order that surrounds him, and of justice and truth and gentleness; than which nothing is more divine, not fire, not light, not the course of the sun, not the risings and settings of the stars, not what is everlasting and immortal. For God is happy not by length of life but by the ruling power of his virtue; for this is divine, and fine too is the part of it that is ruled.

Anaxarchus, then, consoling Alexander when he was in anguish over the murder of Cleitus, said that Zeus too has Justice and Right καὶ τῷ Διὶ - τὴν Θέμιν W: κλείτω δὴ - τὴν τῶν θεῶν as his assessors παρέδρους] cf. Soph. O. C. 1381, so that everything done by a king may seem lawful and just; but it was neither rightly nor helpfully that he tried to cure his remorse for the wrongs he had done, by emboldening him to similar acts. But if one must guess about these things, Zeus does not have Justice as his assessor, but is himself Justice and Right and the oldest and most perfect of laws. The ancients speak and write and teach in that way, implying that without Justice not even Zeus is able to rule well. And she indeed γε] τε Hesiodus (O D. 256) is a virgin, according to Hesiod, uncorrupted, dwelling with reverence and self-restraint and helpfulness ὠφελείας] ἀληθείας codex X as their housemateib. σύνοικος X: ἔνοικος ; hence it is reverendib. αἰδοίους cf. Hom. Δ 402. ς 314 that they call kings; for it is most fitting that those should feel reverence who are least afraid.
But the ruler should fear doing evil more than suffering it; for the one is the cause of the other; and this fear of the ruler is humane and not ignoble, to be afraid on behalf of his subjects lest they be harmed without his knowing,
as dogs keep troubled watch over the sheep in the fold, Hom. K 184
when they hear a stout-hearted wild beast, not for themselves but for those whom they guard. And Epameinondas, when the Thebans had streamed without restraint into a festival and drinking, alone went round the arms and the walls, saying that he was keeping sober and awake so that the others might be free to be drunk and to sleep. And Cato at Utica had it proclaimed that all the others were to be sent from the defeat to the sea; and having put them on board, and having prayed for a good voyage for them, he returned home and slew himself, having taught on whose behalf the ruler must feel fear and whom the ruler must despise. But Clearchus, the tyrant of Pontus, used to creep into a chest like a snake and sleep there. And Aristodemus Ἀριστόδημος] Ἀρίστιππος Vit. Arat. c. 25 of Argos would go into an upper room which had a trap-door, on which ἧς] deleverim he placed his little bed and slept with his mistress; and her mother would draw the ladder away from below, and then in the morning bring it and set it up again. How, do you think, must this man have shuddered at the theatre and the magistrates' hall, the council-chamber, the drinking party, he who had made his bedchamber a prison for himself?
For in truth kings fear for their subjects, but tyrants fear their subjects; therefore they increase their dread along with their power, for ruling more people they fear more.

For it is neither reasonable nor fitting, as some philosophers say, that God is mingled with matter, which suffers everything, and with things which admit countless necessities and chances and changes; but he ὁ μὲν W: ἡμῖν is established somewhere above, in contact with the nature that always remains the same in this way οὕτω] ὠσαύτως R, on holy pedestals, as Plato Πλάτων] de Legg. p. 716a. cf. Phaedr. p. 254 b says, and in a straight εὐθεία R: εὐθέα cf. p. 601b course he reaches his end, proceeding according to nature. And as the sun οἶον δ’ ἥλιος κἑ] fort. corrig. οἶον δ’ ἥλιος ἐν οὐρ. μίμημά τε περικαλλὲς αὐτοῦ καὶ εἲδωλον ἀναφαίνεται cett. deleto δι’ ἐσόπτρου ut glossemate ad δι’ αὐτοῦ (lin. 13); an emendandum δίκην ἐσόπτρου καὶ εἴδωλον?, his most beautiful likeness, appears in heaven as an image in a mirror to those who are able to behold him through it, so he has set up in states the light of justice and of the reason concerning himself αὐτὸν Abreschius: αὐτὴν aut αὐτὸν as an image, which the blessed and the wise copy with the help of philosophy, moulding themselves after the most beautiful of things τῶν παραδειγμάτων M. But nothing produces this disposition except the reason that comes from philosophy, so that we may not suffer what befell Alexander, who, seeing Diogenes in Corinth, and loving him for his natural gifts and admiring the spirit and greatness of the man*: τοῦ ἀνδρὸς , said, If I were not Alexander, I would be Diogenes;
all but δέων] δέω Madvigius. δεῖν Coraes saying that he was burdened by his own αὐτὸν Duebnerus: αὐτὸν good fortune and splendour and power as a hindrance to virtue and a lack of leisure, and that he envied the cloak and the wallet, because by these Diogenes was invincible and impregnable, not, as he himself was, by arms and horses and pikes. So it was possible for him, by practising philosophy, to become Diogenes in disposition and to remain Alexander in fortune, and to become Diogenes all the more because he was Alexander, since for a fortune that was great and had much wind and surge he needed much ballast and a great pilot.

For in the weak and the lowly and private persons, folly, mixed μιγνόμενον] δεδεμένον melius Stob. 46, 102 with lack of power, ends τελευτᾷ] om. mei. Fort. hoc omisso corr. τὸ ἀνόητον εἴργει τὸ ἀμαρτάνειν in doing no wrong, just as inib. ἐν Stobaeus bad dreams a certain distress τις ἀνι **] lac. 7-8 in Amb. 11-12 in V4. τοῖς πάθεσι Stobaeus. Fort. τοῖς ἀνιάτοις πάθεσι troubles the soul, which is unable to rise up together with its desires; but power, taking vice into its hands, adds sinews νεῦρα τοῖς Stobaeus: ἀνιάτοις to the passions, and the saying of Dionysius is true; for he said that he enjoyed his rule most when he quickly did what he wished. Great, then, is the danger that he who is able to do what he wishes may wish what he ought not:
Straightway then indeedib. ἔπειτά γε] ἔπειθ’ ἅμα? was the word, and the deed was accomplished. Hom. T 242
Vice, having through power a swift course, drives out ἐξωθεῖ] ἐξανθεῖ? every passion, making anger murder, love adultery, greed confiscation.
Straightway then, together with it, was the word,Hom. T 242 and the man who gave offence has perished; there is a suspicion, and the man who was slandered is dead. But just as the natural philosophers say that the lightning breaks out later than the thunder, like blood from a wound, but is seen earlier, since the hearing waits for the sound while the sight goes to meet the light; so in governments the punishments anticipate the accusations and the condemnations break out before the proofs.
For now the spirit yields εἴκει p. 446a: ἐκεῖ and no longerib. οὐδʼ eadem: οὐκ holds out, Nauck. p. 911
like an anchor's fluke in the sand in the surge σάλῳ eadem: σάλον (σάλων V2), unless reason, having weight, presses upon and holds down the power, the ruler imitating the sun, which, when it reaches its greatest elevation, lifted up in the northern regions, moves least, making its course safe by its greater slowness.

For it is not possible for vices to escape notice in positions of power; but epileptics, if they come to some height and are carried around, are seized by dizziness and reeling, which exposes their malady, while Fortune, having lifted the uneducated and ignorant up a little with riches or reputations or offices, when they have become exalted at once shows them falling.
Or rather, just as with empty vessels you could not tell the sound one and καὶ] ἢ Coraes the damaged one, but when you pour something in, what leaks becomes visible, so rotten souls, unable to hold power in, leak out in desires, angers, boastings, vulgarities. And yet καίτοι R: καὶ why need one say this, when even the smallest of shortcomings in men who are distinguished and famous become the subject of slander? Wine was the reproach of Cimon, sleep that of Scipio, and Lucullus was ill spoken of for dining too expensively.
